questions.q: What question does monitoring answer, and what question does observability answer, per this lesson?
options: Monitoring answers "why did this fail," and observability answers "is something wrong right now"
Monitoring answers "is something wrong right now," and observability answers "why is it wrong," once monitoring has flagged an issue
They are the same capability described with two different words
Monitoring only applies to synchronous integrations, and observability only to asynchronous ones
questions.explain: Monitoring watches signals and alerts on threshold breaches (is something wrong right now), while observability provides the deeper logged detail and tracing needed to actually diagnose why, once an alert has fired.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe a sudden drop to zero volume as potentially more urgent than a spike in errors?
options: Zero volume always means the integration is working perfectly
Error spikes are never meaningful and should be ignored
Volume has no relationship to whether an integration is healthy
A sudden drop to zero volume can mean the integration silently stopped running altogether — a silent-failure mode that error-count monitoring alone would miss entirely
questions.explain: An integration that silently stops running shows zero errors (because nothing is attempting and failing) while also processing zero volume — exactly the kind of silent failure that only a volume check, not an error-rate check, would catch.

questions.q: For an asynchronous or event-driven integration, what does a backlog/queue depth that only grows over time indicate, and what risk does it eventually create?
options: It indicates consumers aren't keeping up with producers, and it will eventually hit a retention limit and start losing messages if nothing intervenes
It indicates the integration is especially healthy and well-optimized
It has no operational significance and can be safely ignored
It only matters for synchronous, point-to-point integrations
questions.explain: A continuously growing backlog means consumers are falling behind producers; left unaddressed, it will eventually exceed a platform's retention window (such as the Platform Events retention window from Lesson 7) and start losing messages.

questions.q: What does Salesforce's Event Monitoring feature provide, at a conceptual level, per this lesson?
options: It automatically fixes any integration error it detects
A replacement for all Apex debug logs
Detailed event log files covering API usage, login activity, and other platform events, giving visibility into which integration users or connected apps are generating what volume of traffic
A guarantee that no integration can ever exceed a governor limit
questions.explain: Event Monitoring captures detailed log files on API usage and login activity, useful for diagnosing which specific integration or connected app is responsible for a given volume of API traffic or an unexpected traffic pattern change.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against treating "no thrown errors" as proof an integration is healthy?
options: Because thrown errors are always false positives and should be disabled

Because an integration that silently stopped running, one that's succeeding but far slower than before, and one with a silently growing backlog can all show zero errors while being genuinely unhealthy
Because Salesforce does not support error logging of any kind
Because error rate is the only signal that ever matters for integration health
questions.explain: Several real unhealthy states — a stopped integration, degraded latency, or a growing backlog — produce zero thrown errors, which is exactly why monitoring needs to track volume, latency, and backlog explicitly rather than relying on error count alone.
